pois.title: Cape Henry, 1607
pois.text: In April 1607, after four and a half months at sea, 144 English settlers came ashore at the south side of the Bay mouth, put up a wooden cross and named the cape. About three weeks later they founded Jamestown. The granite cross there now was put up in 1935.

pois.title: Battle of the Capes, 1781
pois.text: On 5 September 1781 a French fleet under de Grasse fought 19 British warships off this coast. The British lost 90 men killed and the French kept control of the Bay. With no help able to come by sea, the British army at Yorktown under Cornwallis surrendered on 19 October, a turning point of the American War of Independence.

pois.title: U-boat U-85
pois.text: A German submarine lies about 27 m down off Oregon Inlet. On 14 April 1942 the US destroyer Roper sank it: the first U-boat sunk by US forces off the East Coast in the Second World War.

pois.title: USS Monitor
pois.text: The Union's famous Civil War ironclad sank in a storm off Cape Hatteras on 31 December 1862; 16 of the 62 men aboard died. It lies about 70 m down, and in 1975 the wreck became the first US national marine sanctuary.

pois.title: Sandy Hook Lighthouse, 1764
pois.text: At the mouth of New York harbour stands the oldest lighthouse still working in the United States. It was first lit on 11 June 1764, paid for by a lottery after 43 New York merchants asked for it. The tower is about 103 feet (31 m) tall and its light carries about 19 miles.

pois.title: Block Island Wind Farm
pois.text: Off Block Island, five turbines make up the first offshore wind farm in the United States. Together they make 30 megawatts, and they began commercial operation in December 2016.
pois.source: Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council

pois.title: Steamship Portland, 1898
pois.text: The night steamer Portland left Boston for Portland, Maine on 26 November 1898 and sailed into a storm now called the Portland Gale. Nobody survived: 192 or 193 people died. The wreck lies upright in over 400 feet (120 m) of water in the Stellwagen Bank sanctuary. Found in 1989 and confirmed in 2002, it is called the Titanic of New England.
pois.source: NOAA Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary

pois.title: The Gulf of Maine and the Bay of Fundy
pois.text: This gulf and the Bay of Fundy north of it slosh back and forth about every 13 hours, close to the 12.4 hour beat of the ocean tide, so the tide builds up here. At the head of the bay it can rise more than 16 m (16.1 m was measured at Burntcoat Head). At full flood 25 million cubic metres of water a second pour into the Gulf, about 2,000 times what the St Lawrence river carries.

pois.title: Birchtown, 1783
pois.text: In 1783 about 3,000 Black Loyalists, people who had sided with the British in the American War of Independence, sailed from New York to Nova Scotia. Many settled at Birchtown near Shelburne, then the largest free Black community in British North America. In 1792 about 1,200 of them sailed on to Sierra Leone and founded Freetown.

pois.title: Halifax Explosion, 1917
pois.text: Soon after 9 a.m. on 6 December 1917 the French ship Mont-Blanc, loaded with explosives for the war in Europe, collided with the Norwegian ship Imo in the narrowest part of Halifax harbour. The blast destroyed the north end of the city and raised a tsunami. About 2,000 people died, 9,000 were hurt and 25,000 lost their homes.

pois.title: Sable Island
pois.text: A thin crescent of sand 42 km long and at most 1.3 km wide, 290 km south-east of Halifax. More than 350 ships have been wrecked on and around it, which is why it is called the Graveyard of the Atlantic. Wild horses live there (between 374 and 590 in recent counts), and up to about 80,000 grey seal pups are born on it each winter. It became a national park in 2013.

pois.title: Louisbourg
pois.text: France founded Louisbourg in 1713 to guard its fishing and trade in North America. British forces besieged and took the fortified town twice, in 1745 and 1758. From 1961 to 1981 Parks Canada rebuilt about a quarter of it, the largest rebuilt 18th century French fortified town in North America.

pois.title: The Gulf Stream
pois.text: A river of warm water in the sea, flowing north-east. It averages about 6 km/h and can run near 9 km/h, faster than the kayak's motors push it, and it carries more water than all the world's rivers put together. Further north and east it slows to under 2 km/h.

pois.title: Andrea Doria
pois.text: The Italian liner Andrea Doria was hit in fog by the Swedish liner Stockholm late on 25 July 1956, about 45 miles south of Nantucket. It took 11 hours to sink, long enough for 1,660 people to be rescued; 51 died. The wreck lies about 72 m down.

pois.title: The 'Bermuda Triangle'
pois.text: You're near Bermuda, one corner of the famous triangle. NOAA's answer: ships and planes go missing here no more often than in any busy stretch of ocean, and storms, the Gulf Stream and shallow reefs explain the losses. The name isn't official and there are no official edges.

pois.title: The Sargasso Sea
pois.text: The only sea with no coast: four currents, the Gulf Stream among them, fence it in. Mats of floating seaweed called sargassum give it its name; young turtles shelter in them, and eels and marlin swim here to spawn.

pois.title: Fog off the Grand Banks
pois.text: To the north are the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, where the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream. Where they mix, the fog is famous for lasting days, and the cold current carries icebergs down from Greenland: nearly 500 reach the shipping lanes in an average year.
pois.source: US Coast Guard International Ice Patrol

pois.title: RMS Titanic
pois.text: Not far from here, nearly 4 km down, lies the Titanic. It hit an iceberg and sank on 15 April 1912, about 350 nautical miles off Newfoundland, and more than 1,500 people died. The wreck was found in 1985 by a joint US-French team led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel.

pois.title: The Azores High
pois.text: You're sailing near the Azores High, a big area of high air pressure that usually sits south of the islands. Paired with the Icelandic Low far to the north, it sets the westerly winds across to Europe: the bigger the difference in pressure between them, the stronger the westerlies and the storms.

pois.title: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge
pois.text: You're crossing the seam of the Atlantic. Deep below, the plates of the earth's crust pull apart about 2.5 cm a year, and new sea floor forms between them. Over 100 to 200 million years this spreading grew the Atlantic from a narrow inlet into an ocean.

pois.title: Horta, the cable town
pois.text: Horta on Faial was once a crossroads of the world's telegraph. The first cable reached it in 1893, and by 1928 fifteen undersea cables linked it to Britain, the US, Canada, Ireland, France, Germany, Italy and Cape Verde. The last cable company left in 1969.

pois.title: Azores whalers
pois.text: From Pico and its neighbours, Azoreans hunted sperm whales from open boats with oars, sails and hand-thrown harpoons until 1987. The old whaleboats now race, and the whales bring whale watchers instead.

pois.title: Columbus at Santa Maria, 1493
pois.text: Coming home from his first voyage in February 1493, Columbus was caught by a storm and sheltered at Santa Maria. His men went ashore to give thanks at a shrine, and the unfriendly Portuguese held them for a time. Once freed they sailed on, still in storms, and the battered Niña reached Lisbon.

pois.title: Gorringe Bank
pois.text: A mountain under the sea, about 160 nautical miles off Portugal. It rises from 5,000 m down, and its two peaks, Gettysburg and Ormonde, come to within 50 m of the surface.

pois.title: Cabo da Roca
pois.text: Due east is Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe. A lighthouse has shone there since 1772, and a stone marks it with the poet Camões's line 'where the land ends and the sea begins'.

pois.title: The Lisbon earthquake, 1755
pois.text: On the morning of 1 November 1755 an earthquake of about magnitude 8.7 shook Lisbon, and a tsunami struck the riverfront. About a quarter of the city's 250,000 people died.
